guidance_note: This guide is an independent editorial summary based on the linked official sources checked on 6 November 2026. It is not an offer, endorsement or guarantee of eligibility. Applicants must confirm the current course, nationality, admission, funding and deadline rules with the organiser before applying.

entries.title: Commonwealth Shared Scholarships 2027/28
entries.organisation: Commonwealth Scholarship Commission in the UK
entries.sectors: education, postgraduate study, development, public policy, science, technology
entries.summary: Fully funded one-year taught Master's scholarships in the UK for eligible Commonwealth-country applicants who could not otherwise afford the study. Kenya is on the current eligible-country list. Candidate applications open on 10 November 2026.
entries.support: Approved tuition fees, living-cost support and other scholarship components under the Commonwealth Shared Scholarship terms for selected one-year Master's courses
entries.deadline_label: Opens 10 Nov 2026; closes 8 Dec 2026 at 16:00 GMT
entries.countries: Kenya and other eligible Commonwealth countries including Botswana, Eswatini, Ghana, Lesotho, Malawi, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, Nigeria, Rwanda, Sierra Leone, South Africa, Tanzania, The Gambia, Togo, Uganda and Zambia
benefits: Scholarship support for an approved full-time one-year taught Master's course at a participating UK university.
A development-focused programme intended for applicants who could not otherwise afford UK postgraduate study.
eligibility: Citizen of, or refugee status in, an eligible Commonwealth country and permanently resident in an eligible country; Kenya is listed.

By September 2027, normally hold at least an upper-second-class first degree, or a lower-second-class degree plus a relevant postgraduate qualification, and meet the selected university's admission rules.
conditions: Applicants must apply both for an approved course at a participating university and through the CSC application process; course-specific university deadlines may differ.
Applicants must meet the CSC high-income-country study/work restriction and demonstrate that they cannot afford the UK study without the scholarship.
steps: From 10 November, check the CSC list of approved 2027/28 courses and participating universities.
Apply for the university course and complete the CSC Central application before 16:00 GMT on 8 December 2026.
Prepare degree evidence, references and the development-focused statements required by the CSC and university.
entries.notice: The 2027/28 candidate portal opens on 10 November 2026. Do not use older 2026/27 course lists as the definitive 2027/28 programme list.

guide.context: Commonwealth Shared Scholarships combine UK university participation with Commonwealth Scholarship Commission funding for selected development-focused Master's courses. For Kenyan applicants, the important point is that Kenya is explicitly included in the current eligible-country list, but eligibility is not enough on its own: the applicant also needs an approved course, university admission and a complete CSC application. The 2027/28 candidate window is short, so preparation before the portal opens is useful.
guide.fit: This route is strongest for an applicant with a solid undergraduate record, a clear development problem they want to address after study, and a course choice that connects directly to that problem. It is less suitable for someone seeking an undergraduate degree, PhD, MBA outside the approved list, or a general UK scholarship without a development rationale. Applicants with previous extended study or work in a high-income country should read the restriction carefully before investing time.
prepare: Identify two or three likely approved Master's areas and collect current transcripts and degree certificates.
Draft a concise explanation of the development problem you want to work on in Kenya or your home country and how the selected course builds relevant capability.
Line up referees early and check the participating university's own admission requirements and English-language rules.
Prepare a realistic application calendar covering both university admission and the CSC deadline.
guide.strategy: Treat the university application and scholarship application as two linked processes rather than one form. A credible application should connect prior experience, the chosen course and a specific development contribution without exaggerating impact. Because approved courses are published around the opening period, avoid writing a generic essay for a course that may not appear in the final list. Use the official 2027/28 course list once released and tailor each application to the actual programme.
guide.commitment: If selected, the scholarship is a serious one-year postgraduate commitment in the UK and is intended to build capacity that contributes to development in the applicant's home context. Applicants should plan for the academic intensity, visa process, relocation and the expectation that the study has a clear development purpose. The scholarship should not be treated as a route to bypass course admission requirements or as a guarantee of long-term UK residence.

entries.title: Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters — 2027 intake
entries.sectors: education, postgraduate study, research, international mobility
entries.summary: International joint Master's programmes open to students worldwide, including Kenyan and other African applicants. Many programmes offer full Erasmus Mundus scholarships covering participation costs and contributing to travel, visa and living costs.
entries.support: Programme-dependent full scholarships can cover participation costs and contribute to travel, visa and a living allowance; each consortium sets its own admissions and scholarship process
entries.deadline_label: Programme-specific; most applications are submitted between October and January
entries.countries: Worldwide applicants, including Kenya and all African countries, subject to each Master's programme's academic requirements
benefits: Study in a jointly delivered international Master's involving at least three institutions from at least three countries.
Full scholarships are available in many programmes for the best-ranked applicants and may contribute to participation, travel, visa and living costs.
eligibility: Applicants normally need a Bachelor's degree or must be in the final year and graduate before the Master's starts; recognised equivalent learning may also qualify under programme rules.
Academic prerequisites, language requirements and documents vary by individual Erasmus Mundus consortium.
conditions: There is no single Erasmus Mundus application or universal deadline; applicants apply directly to the consortium running the chosen programme.
Scholarship availability and selection criteria differ by programme, so a course appearing in the catalogue does not mean every applicant receives funding.
steps: Search the official Erasmus Mundus catalogue and shortlist programmes that match your academic background and career direction.
Open each consortium website and record its exact deadline, scholarship rules, document requirements and mobility structure.
Prepare transcripts, degree evidence, references, motivation material and any programme-specific language or portfolio evidence before the individual deadline.
entries.notice: Do not rely on a single January deadline. The European Commission states that most applications fall between October and January, but each Master's consortium controls its own date.
sources: Official Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters student guidance

guide.context: Erasmus Mundus is useful for African applicants because the programme is explicitly global and many joint Master's programmes provide substantial scholarship support. The structure is different from a national scholarship: students apply to a specific consortium, usually study at more than one institution, and follow the admissions and scholarship rules published by that consortium. The strongest advantage is the combination of international academic exposure, mobility and a recognised joint or multiple degree.
guide.fit: A good fit is a graduate whose prior study aligns closely with a listed Master's and who is comfortable with international mobility across institutions or countries. Applicants should look beyond the scholarship headline and check whether the curriculum genuinely fits their academic preparation and goals. Someone needing a single-country, part-time or highly flexible programme may find the multi-institution structure less suitable. Final-year Bachelor's students can often apply if they graduate before the programme begins.
prepare: Use the official catalogue to build a shortlist based on subject fit rather than scholarship value alone.
Create a comparison sheet covering consortium deadline, academic prerequisites, language requirements, scholarship documents and countries of study.
Prepare one strong base CV and evidence pack, then tailor motivation statements to each programme rather than reusing generic text.
Budget time for certified transcripts, references and any language testing requested by the consortium.
guide.strategy: Because each programme controls selection, a disciplined applicant should treat Erasmus Mundus as a portfolio of targeted applications rather than one central competition. Prioritise programmes where your academic record clearly matches the prerequisites and where your motivation can explain why the joint curriculum matters. Check whether a programme has scholarship and self-funded tracks and make sure you select the correct application route. Keep a record of deadlines because several strong programmes may close weeks apart.
guide.commitment: An Erasmus Mundus Master's may involve relocation more than once, intensive coursework, research or traineeship components and compliance with the consortium's mobility plan. Applicants should consider visa sequencing, family responsibilities, housing transitions and the practical demands of studying across countries. A full scholarship is valuable, but the academic and mobility commitment should be acceptable even before funding is considered.

entries.title: Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program at CMU-Africa
entries.organisation: Carnegie Mellon University Africa / Mastercard Foundation
entries.sectors: education, technology, artificial intelligence, engineering, postgraduate study
entries.summary: The Mastercard Foundation currently lists admissions as open at Carnegie Mellon University Africa in Kigali for postgraduate study. The programme supports talented, service-oriented young people facing significant social and economic barriers.
entries.support: Comprehensive Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program support is delivered through CMU-Africa; exact scholarship benefits, admission conditions and current deadlines are controlled by the partner institution
entries.deadline_label: Admissions currently open; confirm the current CMU-Africa application deadline
entries.countries: African applicants; study takes place at CMU-Africa in Kigali, Rwanda, subject to the partner institution's current eligibility rules
benefits: Postgraduate study at CMU-Africa in Information Technology, Electrical and Computer Engineering or Engineering Artificial Intelligence pathways described by the partner.
Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program support is intended for high-achieving young people who face significant barriers to opportunity.
eligibility: Applicants must satisfy CMU-Africa's postgraduate admission requirements and the current Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program selection rules.
The programme emphasises talent, service orientation and applicants facing social or economic barriers; confirm nationality and cohort-specific requirements directly with CMU-Africa.
conditions: The Mastercard Foundation does not select applicants centrally; applications and decisions are managed through partner institutions.
Admission to CMU-Africa does not automatically guarantee selection as a Mastercard Foundation Scholar.
steps: Open the current CMU-Africa Scholars Program and admissions guidance from the official partner page.
Check the exact degree prerequisites, English-language requirements, application deadline and scholarship documents for the current intake.
Prepare academic records, references and evidence of leadership, service and financial need where requested.
entries.notice: The Mastercard Foundation directory marks CMU-Africa admissions as open on 6 November 2026. The partner institution controls the exact deadline and application requirements.
sources: Official Mastercard Foundation CMU-Africa partner page

guide.context: CMU-Africa is an Africa-based postgraduate route in Kigali with a strong technology and engineering focus. The Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program partnership makes it particularly relevant to talented African students who face financial or social barriers and want advanced technical study without leaving the continent. The Foundation's directory currently marks admissions as open, but the university remains responsible for the actual admissions calendar and scholarship selection process.
guide.fit: This opportunity is best suited to applicants with strong preparation for graduate-level technology, engineering or artificial-intelligence study and evidence that they can contribute to their communities or professional field. A compelling applicant should be able to show both academic readiness and a service or leadership orientation. It is not a general scholarship for every discipline, and applicants whose undergraduate preparation does not meet CMU-Africa's technical prerequisites should not assume the scholarship will waive academic requirements.
prepare: Review the exact CMU-Africa degree options and match your undergraduate coursework to the published prerequisites.
Collect transcripts, degree documents, references and any test or language evidence required by the current admissions cycle.
Prepare examples of leadership, community contribution and the barriers that make scholarship support important to your study plan.
Check the current application deadline directly on the university route linked from the official Mastercard Foundation page.
guide.strategy: Start with programme fit, then scholarship fit. A technically strong application should explain why the chosen CMU-Africa programme is the right next step, how prior work demonstrates readiness, and how the applicant intends to use the training in an African context. Avoid relying only on a general statement of financial need. The partner model means applicants should follow CMU-Africa's instructions exactly and should not pay third parties claiming to recruit for the Mastercard Foundation.
guide.commitment: Graduate study at CMU-Africa is a demanding academic commitment in Kigali and may require relocation, full-time study and sustained participation in the Scholars Program community. Applicants should plan around programme duration, living arrangements and any service or leadership expectations. Scholarship support does not reduce the need to meet the academic standard or comply with the university's enrolment requirements.

entries.title: Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program at African Leadership University
entries.sectors: education, undergraduate study, leadership, entrepreneurship, Africa
entries.summary: The Mastercard Foundation currently lists African Leadership University in Kigali as open for undergraduate admissions. The partner programme is aimed at promising young leaders from across Africa who face financial or economic barriers.
entries.support: Full scholarship support through the Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program at ALU, subject to the partner institution's current admissions and scholarship selection rules
entries.deadline_label: Admissions currently open; confirm ALU's current application deadline
entries.countries: Young people from across Africa; study is based at African Leadership University in Kigali, Rwanda, subject to current partner eligibility
benefits: Undergraduate study at African Leadership University with Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program support for selected students.
The partnership emphasises leadership, entrepreneurship, inclusion and access for young Africans facing financial adversity.
eligibility: Applicants must satisfy ALU's current undergraduate admission rules and the Scholars Program's partner-specific selection criteria.
The programme places particular emphasis on promising young African leaders and includes attention to young women, refugees and young people with disabilities.
conditions: Applications are managed by ALU rather than by a central Mastercard Foundation scholarship portal.
Meeting ALU admission requirements does not automatically guarantee scholarship selection; applicants must follow the partner scholarship process.
steps: Review ALU's current degree and admission requirements through the official partner route.
Confirm the active intake deadline and whether the scholarship application is integrated with or separate from admission.
Prepare school records, identity documents and evidence of leadership, initiative, community contribution and financial need as requested.
entries.notice: The official Mastercard Foundation directory marks ALU admissions as open on 6 November 2026. Confirm the exact deadline and cohort rules on ALU's current application page.
sources: Official Mastercard Foundation ALU partner page

guide.context: African Leadership University provides an Africa-based undergraduate route that combines academic study with a strong leadership and entrepreneurial orientation. The Mastercard Foundation partnership is intended to expand access for promising young Africans who face financial barriers. For Kenyan and other African applicants, it can be attractive because the study remains on the continent while offering a regional network and a programme explicitly framed around future African leadership.
guide.fit: A strong applicant is likely to combine academic readiness with evidence of initiative, leadership potential and a clear reason for choosing ALU's educational model. The scholarship is not simply a tuition discount based on grades, and applicants should expect the partner to assess broader potential and barriers to access. Students seeking a conventional programme in a field ALU does not offer should compare alternatives rather than applying only because funding is available.
prepare: Review ALU's current programme catalogue and entry requirements before starting the scholarship process.
Collect school transcripts, identification and any English-language or admissions evidence requested for the active intake.
Prepare concrete examples of leadership, problem-solving, entrepreneurship, service or resilience rather than broad claims.
Check the current application deadline and scholarship steps on the university route linked by the Mastercard Foundation.
guide.strategy: The application should show fit with ALU's model and the Scholars Program's access purpose at the same time. Explain what you have already tried to do in your school, community or area of interest, what you learned and why the ALU programme would expand your capability. Avoid paying unofficial agents or responding to social-media accounts asking for scholarship fees; the Mastercard Foundation directs applicants to its partner institutions.
guide.commitment: Undergraduate study in Kigali requires a multi-year commitment and active participation in an institution that emphasises leadership and enterprise. Applicants should consider relocation, academic workload, the social environment and how the programme connects to their long-term plans. A scholarship decision remains separate from admission, and all final terms should be confirmed directly with ALU.

entries.title: AERC Industrial Policy and Growth in Africa Research Call
entries.sectors: research, economics, industrial policy, manufacturing, agro-processing, regional integration
entries.summary: AERC is commissioning policy-relevant studies on industrialisation in Africa, with a focus on early-career African and Africa-focused economists. Each selected study can receive up to US$10,000.
entries.support: Up to US$10,000 per commissioned study for researcher time, secondary data access and software; primary data collection and field travel are excluded
entries.countries: Early-career African and Africa-focused economists; research must address industrial policy and growth questions relevant to Africa
benefits: Up to US$10,000 for each commissioned study and an 18-month research work plan.
Opportunity to produce policy-relevant research and high-quality academic outputs on African industrialisation.
eligibility: The call targets early-career African and Africa-focused economists; applicants should check the current PhD timing and team-composition requirements in the full guidelines.
Proposals must address one of the project's specified industrial-policy questions and demonstrate access to suitable data.
conditions: Primary data collection and field travel are not funded; the proposal must rely on appropriate existing data and show evidence of access.
The proposal is capped at 2,000 words excluding CVs, the budget table and references, and must follow the specified structure.
steps: Read the AERC themes and choose a research question that fits the call rather than submitting a generic economics proposal.
Prepare the 2,000-word proposal, CVs, proof of PhD award date, an 18-month timeline and a budget of no more than US$10,000.
Submit through the AERC Research and Capacity Development Portal before the stated East Africa Time deadline.
entries.notice: AERC's detailed timeline states 21 November 2026 at midnight EAT; applicants should follow the programme page and portal if any summary listing shows a different date.
sources: Official AERC Research and Capacity Development Portal call

guide.context: This AERC call is a genuine research commissioning opportunity rather than a scholarship or general grant. It seeks rigorous evidence on why African industrialisation remains constrained and how policy affects firms, investment, regional integration and value addition. The research is intended to be publishable and policy-relevant, and the call specifically emphasises early-career researchers. For Kenya-based economists and other African researchers, the East Africa Time deadline and Africa-wide subject matter make it particularly accessible if the methodological and data requirements are already in place.
guide.fit: The strongest applicant is an early-career economist with a completed PhD within the call's permitted window, a research question closely aligned to one of AERC's themes and access to suitable secondary data before submission. Teams should be able to execute an identification strategy without relying on fieldwork that the grant will not finance. A proposal that mainly requests money to collect new primary data, or that addresses industrial policy only loosely, is unlikely to fit the stated design.
prepare: Select the exact call question and assemble the data you intend to use before writing the proposal.
Prepare a short descriptive summary showing that the data exist and are adequate for the proposed empirical strategy.
Draft the proposal within the stated section and word limits, including an 18-month work plan and budget capped at US$10,000.
Attach short CVs and proof of the PhD award date for the relevant researchers.
guide.strategy: Use the proposal space to demonstrate feasibility and identification rather than spending most of the word count on broad background. AERC explicitly asks for data, methodology, expected outputs and a publication strategy. Make the policy relevance to African industrial development concrete and show why the proposed evidence can change a real policy or research debate. Because primary data collection is excluded, the data-access claim should be credible and verifiable at submission time.
guide.commitment: A commissioned study is an 18-month research obligation, not a one-off prize. Applicants should be prepared to manage the research timetable, produce the agreed outputs and engage with AERC's academic and policy expectations. The US$10,000 ceiling should be treated as a research budget with defined eligible purposes rather than unrestricted personal income.

entries.title: Research Continuity Grants for Africa
entries.sectors: research, natural sciences, crisis recovery, universities, Africa
entries.summary: Six grants of up to US$2,000 support African scientists at recognised universities or research institutions in Africa to resume or complete natural-sciences research interrupted by conflict or natural or biological hazards.
entries.support: Six grants of up to US$2,000 each to help eligible African scientists resume or complete interrupted natural-sciences research
entries.deadline_label: 15 Nov 2026; confirm the exact cutoff time on the official call
entries.countries: African scientists based at recognised universities or research institutions in Africa whose natural-sciences work was interrupted by conflict or natural or biological hazards
benefits: Up to US$2,000 for one of six supported research-continuity grants.
A crisis-response mechanism intended to help interrupted natural-sciences research resume or reach completion.
eligibility: Applicant must be an African scientist based at a recognised university or research institution in Africa and meet the crisis-interruption criteria in the official call.
The research must be in the natural sciences and have been interrupted by conflict or a natural or biological hazard.
conditions: This is a narrowly targeted continuity grant, not a general research-funding call for any African scientist.
Only six grants are available, so applicants should document the interruption, remaining research need and realistic use of the limited award.
steps: Read the current UNESCO/TWAS call and confirm that the cause of interruption and research field fit the eligibility rules.
Prepare evidence of institutional affiliation, the interrupted project, the remaining work and the budget needed to resume or complete it.
Submit through the official application route before the 15 November date and confirm the exact cutoff time shown in the live portal.
entries.notice: The opportunity is designed for research interrupted by crisis or hazard. Scientists whose work was not interrupted for one of the stated reasons should use other TWAS research or fellowship routes.
sources: TWAS Research and Project Grants page

guide.context: The Research Continuity Grants for Africa are unusually specific. They are not intended to launch a new research programme; they are designed to help African scientists whose natural-sciences work was disrupted by conflict or a natural or biological hazard. The award size is modest, but for a project close to completion it may be useful for essential consumables, access or other bounded needs that can restart work quickly. Applicants should read the crisis criterion as a core eligibility condition, not as background language.
guide.fit: A strong fit is a scientist at a recognised African university or research institution who can show an identifiable natural-sciences project, a qualifying interruption and a realistic plan to resume or finish the work with a small grant. It is not a fit for social-science research, general tuition, a new unrelated project or an applicant simply facing ordinary funding constraints. The limited number of awards also means the explanation of disruption and continuity should be precise.
prepare: Document the original research project, its institutional home and the point at which work was interrupted.
Explain the conflict, natural hazard or biological hazard that caused the interruption without overstating or broadening the event.
Build a small, practical budget showing exactly how the requested amount will restart or complete the research.
Confirm the live application form's required institutional letters, CV or project evidence before submission.
guide.strategy: The proposal should focus on continuity: what was already underway, what stopped, what remains and why a small intervention can produce a meaningful research outcome. Avoid rewriting the project as a completely new study. If the requested work requires substantially more than the award ceiling or depends on major new fieldwork, another TWAS or institutional funding route may be more realistic.
guide.commitment: Successful applicants should be ready to use a small award efficiently and complete the stated research-continuity objective. Institutional affiliation and scientific integrity remain important even though the funding is emergency-oriented. Applicants should retain documentation of expenditures and outputs required by the organiser and should not assume that a continuity grant creates a pathway to larger automatic TWAS funding.
